I was elected to Congress in 2020 after founding and running a public middle school in the Bronx for ten years. I've spent my entire career as an advocate for communities that have been ignored and abused, first as an educator and now as an elected o[icial. In Congress I've brought back over a billion dollars to my district, with new investments in local gun violence prevention programs, a[ordable housing, health care, climate action, and more. What are your policy priorities if you are to win this seat? How will these policy priorities impact the LGBTQ community? My policy priorities are the protection of basic rights for all people. The rights to education, to housing, and to healthcare. The right to live in safety and dignity. I want the federal government to make major investments in public schools and the care economy, and to take on the far right extremists who want to take away our basic rights. These policies are broadly important for everyone, but I think can bring tremendous benefit to the LGBTQ community. [PDF page 63] 2024 Federal Endorsement Questionnaire Jamaal Bowman US House of Representatives 16 Section 3 - Critical Issues Across the nation, and in New York State, we have seen a massive wave of anti LGBTQ legislation, including restricting rights of trans youth, bans on LGBTQ books in schools, limits on drag queen performances, and limits on gender aAirming care for minors and adults. How would you use your platform as a Member of Congress to advocate for protection of LGBTQ people across the city, state and country? The far right is trying to advance a disgusting anti-LGBTQ agenda in Congress and in state and local governments across the country. There are a few ways I use my platform to fight back. First is always speaking with a loud and clear voice to defend the rights of LGBTQ people on the floor of the House, at events in my district, and in the media. There is no compromise with people who want to take away our rights. The second is through legislation. I'm proud to have co-sponsored a large amount of bills centering protections for LGBTQ people, many of which are noted in this questionnaire. And the last thing is by being active in my district with organizations of and for the LGBTQ community, and helping them get federal funding. From shelters for trans youth to advocacy groups like The LOFT in White Plains, I've been a consistent ally in Congress. The LGBTQ community has historically been over policed, and research shows that law enforcement continues to disproportionately target marginalized people: What do you view as the US Congress’s role in ensuring law enforcement oversight, funding, and the needs of marginalized communities? What, if any, relevant policy proposals do you support regarding law enforcement? I have very strong views on the appropriate role for the law enforcement agencies and the need for much stricter accountability and oversight around law enforcement in marginalized communities. This is personal for me. I grew up in public housing in New York City, in working class Black communities where the police were a constant threat to my life and the lives of everyone I cared about. We need to end the school to prison pipeline, end qualified immunity, and end the flow of military weapons to local law enforcement, and pass the George Floyd Justice in Policing Act. I would love to work in closer partnership with LGBTQ advocates around criminal justice reform. New York State is experiencing a housing crisis and the LGBTQ community disproportionately experiences homelessness, especially our LGBTQ youth and seniors. How do we ensure that any plan is equitable to the LGBTQ Community and other marginalized groups? New York State is facing a housing crisis and as always, crises fall heaviest on the most marginalized among us. It is essential that any solutions to the crisis center those folks first, including LGBTQ youth and seniors. We absolutely need to build more housing but we need to be building housing that is truly a[ordable, and alongside a[ordable housing we need full funding for supportive housing of all kinds. The federal funding I have won back for my district includes $2M for Bronx students living in shelters and 4

[PDF page 64] 2024 Federal Endorsement Questionnaire Jamaal Bowman US House of Representatives 16 $1.6M for the YouthHEAL program, and $800k for senior housing in the Northeast Bronx, among so many other examples. With the repeal of Roe V. Wade and states across the country implementing abortion bans, New York State has become a safe haven for reproductive rights. In today’s political landscape, what would you do as a Member of Congress to protect and expand reproductive healthcare? The repeal of Roe was a terrifying moment, as I know the dangerous and deadly repercussions pregnant people will face in many states. I will continue to fight for New York as a safe haven, but that's not enough. I will fight to bring Democrats back into the majority in November and then the top of our priorities needs to be passing the Access to Abortion Act, expanding the Supreme Court, and creating truly universal healthcare that covers abortions. Co-sponsor "H.R. 3850, the Pride in Mental Health Act The Pride in Mental Health Act works to close LGBTQI+ mental health information gaps and improve physical and mental health in at-risk youth." Co-sponsor "H.R. 3970, the LGBTQI+ Data Inclusion Act This bill addresses federal data collection of voluntary, self-disclosed information on sexual orientation, gender identity, and variations in sex characteristics. Specifically, the bill requires federal agencies that collect information through a survey for statistical purposes that includes demographic data (where subjects self-report information or a proxy provides information about the subject or responds for all 5

It permits such couples to amend their filing status to married filing jointly for tax returns outside of the statute of limitations and modifies tax rules relating to married couples to include same sex couples." Please explain any activities and/or experiences that demonstrate your commitment to the LGBT civil rights movement. Du Bois spoke about being black in America as having a “double-consciousness,” and I can say growing up as the black American child of Eritrean immigrants that I felt a triple-consciousness. There can be extreme trauma and difficulty in growing up and living in America as a first-generation black person: from Eritrean cultural dislocation to coming to terms with a white supremacist history of exploitation. The fact that many of our parents don’t have language or awareness to help us navigate the problems of race and racism here can exacerbate our struggle. But there is also a blessing that comes from being racialized into marginalization: the opportunity and necessity for radical empathy. Even if they were not all directly my histories, I felt the pain of slavery, segregation, racism, genocide, and colonialism in me

[PDF page 2] 2020 Congressional Candidate Questionnaire Responses as a black person. I knew how hypocritical it would be for me to, even latently, support any system of oppression, when I understood the feeling of being oppressed myself. I certainly don’t believe blackness or a group’s history of marginalization is a prerequisite for radical empathy, but, for me, this understanding helped me unpack my own privilege at a young age, helped me stand in solidarity with other oppressed groups, and helped serve as a foundation for my own activism and work in education. It bestowed upon me a liberatory politics that critiqued and questioned a status quo built on and sustained by imperialism, racism, heteropatriarchy, and economic exploitation, and affirmed that the artifice of stability should never preclude people’s right to freedom, equality, and justice. I became aware of the LGBT civil rights movement after the brutal murder of Matthew Shephard. As a young teenager, I became aware of the ways homophobic language was normalized in the communities I grew up in, and I challenged it anywhere I heard it. When I became a teacher, I ensured LGBTQ+ histories were included in my curriculum, and I helped create accountable interventions with social workers around transphobic and homophobic bullying. An understanding of universal human rights and indivisible justice for all were at the center of my curriculum and discipline protocol, which afforded a frame for respecting and acknowledging difference, developing tolerance, and building empathy. What experience do you have to demonstrate you are the best person to represent the office you seek? I am a first-generation American, a product of Eritrean immigrants, a brother, a proud Mount Vernon resident, a special education teacher, a Knicks fan. As a child, I internalized my parents’ revolutionary efforts in support of Eritrean liberation and connected it to the struggles for recognition and inclusion in the worlds I knew. Growing up in Mount Vernon, I was exposed to inequality around all me. The contradictions apparent in the different communities I was steeped in provoked a justice-seeking politics within me and has informed my professional career. I graduated from Yale with degrees in Political Science and Economics and then CCNY with a Master’s in Secondary Special Education. I became a special education teacher largely because of the inequities I saw in different school systems growing up. I have now been in education for over 10 years (in the Bronx, Washington Heights, and Palestine). School can be a site of liberation and discovery, but, for most of my students, school put them in the pipeline to prison instead of a path to college. I am proud that – in my classroom – I was able to provide a safe space for my students to holistically develop their intelligences, while giving them the critical tools to question not only what they learn but their position in society.

[PDF page 3] 2020 Congressional Candidate Questionnaire Responses As teachers, we not only manage 35 teenagers in underfunded classrooms daily, we get our young people to believe in themselves when the world has told them they shouldn’t. Teaching special education in NYC, I had to demystify education for many of my students, some who entered my 8th grade class on a 1st grade reading level. They’ve been failed every step of the way, so when they arrive in my class, my job is to create a plan in concert with them and a host of diverse stakeholders in the community - social workers, parents, coaches, religious leaders – to ensure they progress. Collaborating to implement needed interventions is exactly what I will be doing in Congress for communities that have been underserved and neglected for too long and for a country that has as little faith in government as my students did in school. Why I’m Running? I am running for office because the district I have known my whole life is not best served by a militaristic Democrat like Eliot Engel. I taught in my district in an underfunded, segregated school, where my 12-year olds walked through metal detectors at 7:45 AM into a school that had 1 social worker for 500 students. It became irreconcilable to me that this was our unabating reality while our public money was being diverted to unnecessary wars. Our community is more concerned with investments in education, health care, housing, and jobs than wasteful military spending. We are focusing on fighting climate change and securing a Global Green New Deal, but that’s only possible if we divest from the military industrial complex and pursue the multilateralism necessary to have the world aligned on shared climate goals. Engel has been in Congress for 30 years, rising to the Chair of House Foreign Affairs, and he's been one of the leading Democratic proponents of an immoral foreign policy our district is against: voting for the Iraq War, opposing Obama’s Iran deal, stonewalling action against Saudi Arabia in Yemen, and challenging efforts to hold the Israeli government accountable. I am running because, as my students’ families are struggling here, and our cousins are dying in US-wars abroad, these hawkish Democrats can no longer represent us. The imperialist militarization of US foreign policy weakens democracy at home. Fighting the entrenchment of the police state, deportation apparatus, and mass surveillance, as well as increasing white nationalism, necessitates championing a progressive foreign policy. Such a foreign policy vision provides the moral foundation and fiscal flexibility to advocate for social programs that deepen our democracy, secure working people’s freedom, and guarantee rights/justice for historically marginalized groups. Please detail any specific policy proposals you may have that will affect the LGBT community. The LGBTQ+ community has historically been disproportionately affected by housing and workplace discrimination, but, in this era of Trump, anti-LGBTQ+ violence is rapidly

In 2018, for example, at least 26 trans people were murdered, the majority of whom were black women. We demand an end to the violence, and we will continue to fight for full equality for all LGTBQ+ people. We will fight against discrimination in housing, employment, and public settings and work to ensure that our education system promotes inclusivity and has programs targeting homophobic and transphobic bullying. • Support the Equality Act, which would prohibit discrimination due to sexual orientation and/or gender identity as detailed in Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 • Support LGBTQ-inclusive education (curricular inclusion; programs to counter anti-LGBTQ bullying; LGTBQ-specific counseling and support; training and professional development for staff; the Safe Schools Improvement Act, the Student Non- Discrimination Act, the Tyler Clementi Higher Education Anti-Harassment Act, and the Real Education for Healthy Youth Act) • End the Trump administration’s ban on trans military service • De-gender public facilities • Ban conversion therapy nationwide • Repeal "Walking While Trans" Ban • Guarantee trans-affirming healthcare • Ban intersex mutilation • End discrimination in HHS programs, specifically with adoption and foster care agencies • Decriminalize migration, sex work, and "crimes of poverty" • Support Medicare for All and protect the right and access to a safe, unrestricted abortion for all women, trans men, and non-binary people Section 3: FEDERAL POLICY POSITIONS (yes or no) Legislation and Policies SDNYC Supports: Do you support enshrining and continuing anti-discrimination protections for these classes of individuals from discrimination in all its forms: race, color, national origin, and in most cases,

Last week, my advocacy to free Chin Mei Tsui from ICE custody succeeded when Gov. Cuomo granted Chin a pardon, and ICE subsequently released him. I am currently working to ensure that every family in the country has access to paid family leave, building on my work to include LGBTQ+ families in these policies both in Congress and, previous to that, as a member of the NYC city council.

I have served in Congress since 1993, and over that time have achieved a number of things for NY-12 and NYC. Most recently, that includes passing the 9/11 Victims Compensation Fund, obtaining funding for major public infrastructure projects, including L-train repairs and the Kosciuszko Bridge, fighting for the Equal Rights Amendment, passing consumer protection measures for corporate board diversity and ending unfair banking practices, and finding ways to address our district and country's growing inequality. Having represented the community throughout my career, I have a firm understanding of the issues that matter in NY-12 - and have the experience and knowledge of how to work within the system to address those issues. Having built a publicly-funded health care system with the 9/11 programs, I know we can fight for and win Medicare for All while protecting the ACA - and the 135 million Americans who depend on it - from GOP sabotage. As a lifelong advocate for the environment, I fought to get Newtown Creek declared a superfund site and have pushed for better environmental standards and corporate responsibility towards the environment - and now I am an original co-sponsor on the Green New Deal, because we must address the climate crisis NOW. I have fought for NYCHA and affordable housing, and am a co-sponsor on the Green New Deal for Public Housing. Last year, I became the first woman elected to chair the House Committee on Oversight and Reform, and that has enabled me to shine a national spotlight on some of our most pressing issues. One of my first actions was to impeach Donald Trump, and I've kept up the pressure on his administration since then with demands for financial documents and other records that would show the extent of his corruption. In addition, I've already held hearings on inclusive, universal paid family leave, on the ways in which the Trump administration is using religion to discriminate against LGBTQ+ Americans, on states' draconian laws opposing abortion access, on the cruel border policies this administration has enacted, and most recently, a two-day hearing on the administration's lackluster response to the Coronavirus, among other topics. Please detail any specific policy proposals you may have that will affect the LGBT community. Last year, we passed the Equality Act in the Senate - we will continue to work to pass this bill and safeguard these vital protections for our LGBTQ+ friends and neighbors. I am also working to ensure the Trump administration cannot misuse "religious exemptions" to create a license to discriminate against LGBTQ+ people. I also recently

This piece of legislation ensures that schools are adequately resourced with guidance counselors and social workers to ensure that every school is a safe haven for kids regardless of background or orientation or identity. My work with AQE and others seeks to ensure that our schools are trauma informed and effective at implementing restorative justice practices. What experience do you have to demonstrate you are the best person to represent the office you seek? When I was a little kid, my grandmother and my mother raised me in NYC public housing. I grew up with kids of every background, and it changed my life, all of us a short walk away from excellent schools and museums. When I got older, I thought about how things could have been different if I had never met those kids, and if my mom never found a union job. I chose to become a teacher because I wanted every kid in our city to have a chance to grow up the way I did. Ten years ago, I founded a public middle school in the Bronx, the Cornerstone Academy for Social Action, where I served as the principal until the end of 2019. I built this school based on the principles of equity and restorative justice. My goal has been to create an environment that supports the whole child, fostering their emotional wellbeing and unique interests, all while teaching standard subject matter and working to dismantle the school-to-prison pipeline. I know this work could dramatically change historically oppressed communities nationwide if it were given the platform to do so. I’m proud of our work at CASA, but there’s only so much we can do within a single school. After two decades in public education, I am tired of watching our families struggle to live a good life because they can’t get jobs, health care, housing, the dignity and safety they need. I am tired of seeing hedge funds try to buy out our public school system through privatization. I’ve had enough of a generation of politicians who underfunded our schools and cut our social safety net while building more jails, bailing out Wall Street, accepting corporate PAC donations, and spending trillions of dollars on never-ending wars. Our district is more progressive and diverse than ever, but Representative Engel is a leader who represents the past and isn’t doing enough to build urgency and organize a movement to transform our democracy. Along with many issues at the national level, Engel failed to side with the WFP and other members of Congress who endorsed challengers taking on the rogue IDC. Paying workers who have not been recognized by society for their labor such as caregivers would also foster a stronger, and more sustainable community. As an entrepreneur with my startup company Brightbox, I partnered with dozens of LGBT owned and centered restaurants and bars in NYC, LA, SF, and Miami. What experience do you have to demonstrate you are the best person to represent the office you seek? We need a representative who understands how to battle the great issues of our time that COVID19 has put into stark reality: economic inequality, racial injustice, and climate disaster. I believe we can do that by fighting for homerenters, for workers, and for cities. I am uniquely prepared to do that. I have lived in this district for 14 years. Over that time I have been a housing activist and policy writer, a professor and rank and file union member at Baruch College, and an entrepreneur who has co-founded two startup companies. I have the values, the relationships, and the experience necessary on Day One to make the progressive policy changes necessary to serve the needs for all residents in NY-12 today and in the future. Here are my three focuses: -72% of NY12 residents are homerenters; I have been on the frontline of the affordable housing crisis as a tenant organizer with the Stuytown Tenants Association and have personally fought multiple bogus eviction notices in housing court. I became the senior housing policy advisor with Data for Progress and advised on multiple presidential housing plans and helped write the Homes Guarantee platform that creates a concrete roadmap to make housing a human right. I am on the leading edge of housing policy thought at the national level and have the relationships in and out of government to push for the progessive agenda we need. -44% of NY12 residents are under 40 and have prohibitive debt and wage insecurity. I have experienced this as an adjunct at Baruch College and rank and file member of PSC-CUNY union who has fought for better wages for staff and more resources for students; as a bartender and grad student working without health insurance or a predictable schedule; and as an entrepreneur who has co-founded two companies without subsidies from the Empire State Development Corp. I’ve outlined a New Economy of Care, which is a plan to empower all workers, allow them to benefit from technology by working less while making more, and by centering families and communities over shareholders and corporations. As an entrepreneur and an Information Technology professor at a business school I have the credibility and the experience to advocate for rebooting our economy to work for all of us. -Over 75% of carbon emissions come from our buildings and transportation system. COVID19 is just a dress rehearsal for climate disaster and we are not prepared. I have

The LGBTQ civil rights movement is baked into every fiber of my being. Former Co-President, Lambda, Harvard Law School Founding Team (6th hire), Andrew Yang 2020 Campaign Fellow, Senior Advisor & Counselor, Office of the New York State Attorney General Fellow, Mayday.US, Larry Lessig’s “Super PAC to end all Super PACs” What experience do you have to demonstrate you are the best person to represent the office you seek?: I am a grassroots organizer, educator, and advocate for universal basic income endorsed by Andrew Yang. I am running to fight for deep freedom, not shallow equality. To raise the floor, not lower the ceiling. To fix the system, not find others to blame. We're going through the greatest economic and technological shift in our history and need to urgently pass 21st century solutions to these 21st century problems. We need a Representative who understands the structural crises we’re facing and has a clear vision and track record to tackle them. Before COVID-19, in New York's 10th District, the world's financial capital, 1 in 6 lived in poverty. Before COVID-19, in New York's 10th District, 20

[PDF page 83] 2020 Congressional Candidate Questionnaire Responses percent of storefronts were closing. Before COVID-19, in New York City, there were more than 4,600 homeless youth, almost entirely people of color and nearly half LGBTQ. I went to Hunter College High School, graduated first in my class at Harvard, and completed my MBA at NYU Stern. I served as co-President of Student Government at Harvard Law School, where I am a teaching fellow for legal and political philosophy. I was part of the founding team of Andrew Yang’s 2020 presidential campaign, joining the campaign as the 6th hire, building the Iowa operation from the ground up, and leading Andrew’s rise as the “internet candidate.” We are in the midst of a global pandemic and the fourth industrial revolution. Economic projections are worse than The Great Depression. After automating away millions of the most common jobs and pushing tens of millions into economic insecurity, more than 22 million Americans are now unemployed and more than 40,000 are dead due to COVID-19. Congress is still on recess. More than 1 million New Yorkers are unemployed, and more than 10,000 have died in New York City alone. Congress is still on recess. We need to wake up. Hate crimes in New York doubled in 2019 alone. It's not about Trump. It’s about what comes next. I did not set out to run for Congress. I reached out to the most prominent civil rights leaders, politicians, journalists, and academics to sound the alarm about the urgency of a universal basic income – a message first championed by Martin Luther King Jr. – but eventually realized that for anything to change we had to “build a wave and bring it crashing down on their heads.” Once I grasped the scale of the problems we face, and reckoned with the reality that no politician was going to do much about it, I had to act. I took an indefinite leave from Harvard Law School to join the founding team for 2020 Democratic Presidential Candidate Andrew Yang's campaign, helping build the grassroots movement from the ground up and bring universal basic income to the mainstream. The likes of Barack Obama, Hillary Clinton, Bernie Sanders, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, members of the Trump administration, Justin Amash, Mitt Romney, Dan Savage, Sam Altman, Elon Musk, Dave Chappelle, Donald Glover, and Whoopi Goldberg, now support some version of a universal basic income. Before the Nazi rise to power, the Holocaust, and the systematic slaughter of tens of thousands of homosexuals, Theodor Wolff in 1933 remarked: “It’s a hopeless mis-judgement to think that one could force a dictatorial regime upon the German nation. [Our] diversity calls for democracy.” Little did Wolff know that democracy itself would soon bring dictatorship. Nazi seats in the Reichstag had an almost one-to-one correlation with the level of German unemployment once it surpassed 30 percent. The Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis a few weeks ago projected 32 percent unemployment. Here. In the United States. In 2020. As Yuval Harari, the gay historian, said in 2019: today, “whoever controls the algorithms [is]

[PDF page 84] 2020 Congressional Candidate Questionnaire Responses the real government.” As the Humanity Forward movement caught fire, the same question came up over and over again: how will we get Congress to pass universal basic income, universal healthcare, data property rights, public funding of elections, ranked-choice voting, and the entire Humanity Forward agenda? This is my answer. It would be an honor to earn your support on June 23rd. Please detail any specific policy proposals you may have that will affect the LGBT community.: The promise that “It Gets Better” is hollow without the promise of financial security in the case your family or community rejects you for who you are. We, the LGBTQ community, are tragically overrepresented among foster children, the homeless, the poor, and the food-insecure. 1 in 5 LGBTQ Americans lives in poverty. 1 in 6 people in New York's 10th District live in poverty. Poverty is an absence of cash, not character. LGBTQ youth are kicked out by our parents at a higher rate than the general population. Fifteen percent of transgender people, and more than 30 percent of trans people of color, are living in severe poverty. The Freedom Dividend (a Universal Basic Income of $1,000/month for every adult and $500/month for every child) would disproportionately benefit LGBTQ youth, especially LGBTQ kids of color, and give us all the freedom to live full, authentic lives. The single most transformative way for the government to improve the lives of the LGBTQ community is to send us a check for $1,000 every month and let us spend it in whatever manner will benefit us the most. We need to build a new kind of economy – one that puts people first. If there’s one policy that would transform the lives of LGBTQ Americans for the better, it is Universal Basic Income. Universal basic income does not solve every problem, but it makes every problem easier to solve. I would of course also fight to extend legal non-discrimination protections for our community. Sexual orientation and gender identity should be protected classes under the law, receiving all the federal protections afforded under the Constitution and civil rights law. We must also publicly fund our elections, pass federal ranked-choice voting, restore voting rights protections, and fight for fundamental democracy reform so that the LGBTQ community and our needs will be reflected in the halls of Congress. Healthcare should be a basic right for all Americans. I am for Universal Healthcare and expanding Medicare to cover all Americans. Too many Americans, especially in the LGBTQ community, are making terrible, impossible choices between paying for healthcare and other needs. We need to provide high-quality healthcare to all Americans and moving towards a

[PDF page 85] 2020 Congressional Candidate Questionnaire Responses single-payer system is the most efficient way to accomplish that. It will be a massive boost to our economy as people will be able to start businesses and change jobs without fear of losing their health insurance. A big but underserved part of healthcare is mental health. New Yorkers, especially LGBTQ New Yorkers, are not doing well and we need to change that. A recent survey of thousands of LGBTQ youth showed what we know all to well - heartbreaking levels of stress, anxiety, rejection, and feeling unsafe in school. Integrating mental health with our greater health care system is a top priority - if someone comes to the hospital suffering from diabetes, obesity or substance abuse, there is often a link to their holistic mental health. Please explain any activities and/or experiences that demonstrate your commitment to the LGBT civil rights movement. I have a long track record of commitment to LGBTQIA+ liberation. I personally identify as a part of the LGBTQIA+ community and have fought for decades for health, dignity and justice for LGBTQIA+ people, particularly immigrants, Latinxs and queer people of color. In my community, I have long supported LGBTQIA+ leaders and organizations, and have participated in our local Queens Pride parade since 2001 - marching either as a former elected official (Democratic State Committee Member), or with organizations, such a New Immigrant Community Empowerment (NICE). In the late ‘90s/early 2000s, I showed up alongside the LGBTQIA+ community in Queens when Julio Rivera and Edgar Garzon were separately murdered in Jackson Heights, attending vigils and events that honored their lives, and worked with (then-District Leader) Danny Dromm and the Garzon family to demand that the police investigate Edgar’s murder. I have always supported and championed policies that advance the civil rights of the LGBTQIA+ community and as the former leader of the National Latina Institute for Reproductive Justice, I ensured that all our policy work incorporated an LGBTQIA+ lens. For example, we were one of the first reproductive justice organizations to serve as bold advocates for the reproductive health needs of Latinx trans men,

[PDF page 12] 2020 State Candidate Questionnaire Responses noting that dignified gynecological care, pap smears and birth control were health services that trans men needed access to, and we fought to ensure it was also culturally-competent, linguistically appropriate and accessible, despite immigration status. Another policy priority was fighting for the civil rights provision of the Affordable Care Act (section 1557) which included sexual orientation and gender identity as protected classes. I’ve invested sponsorship funding and served on committees for the Latinx Pre-Conference Institute of Creating Change Conference (the largest LGBTQ annual conference in the country) and regularly presented on panels regarding the intersections of LGBTQIA+ liberation, reproductive justice and immigration, once serving as a plenary speaker. I’ve served on countless coalitions alongside LGBTQIA+ organizations, hosted numerous congressional briefings on LGBTQIA+ health, written op-eds advocating for queer-friendly policies and thought pieces on intersectionality (here is 2012 example from the Huffington Post: https://www.huffpost.com/entry/latino-lgbtq_b_1640055) and have built deep partnerships with leaders across movements. Lastly, I ensure my organization’s policies and practices aligned with values that we promoted and that such policies that used language that was gender-neutral and inclusive, such as ‘parental leave’ instead of ‘maternity leave.’ I am proud to have hired queer- identified and trans staff throughout the organization, serving in both leadership and management positions. This is the approach I plan to take forward into the New York State Assembly. What experience do you have to demonstrate you are the best person to represent the office you seek? As the daughter of an immigrant father from Paraguay and a Puerto Rican mother, I am a fierce advocate for people of color, immigrants, and LGBTQIA+ communities. Corona, East Elmhurst, Jackson Heights, and Woodside - the communities of the 34th Assembly District - are among the most diverse neighborhoods in the world. I understand that the strength of our Queens community is in its diversity, and I hold an unwavering commitment to progressive values. Through my community activism on immigration, I’ve witnessed the challenges that everyday families face when looking to secure stable housing, raise children, seek dignified work, and succeed in this country. And through my advocacy on gender and reproductive justice, I see how laws deeply impact our ability to make autonomous decisions about our bodies, health, family, and future. I am running for State Assembly because I am an activist both locally and nationally with a proven track record of standing up and speaking out against injustices. For the past 13 years, I have served as the leader of the National Latina Institute for Reproductive Health, an organization dedicated to building Latina power to advance gender justice, becoming a nationally recognized

[PDF page 13] 2020 State Candidate Questionnaire Responses advocate for universal health care and reproductive freedom. It takes a leader who understands and connects to the experiences and struggles of our community to be an effective representative. I am running for State Assembly because we deserve a choice in who represents us. For too long, we have been represented by someone who was handpicked by the party bosses in a rigged process that shut voters out. The incumbent has never had to face a challenger and who does not reflect our values or our diversity. The voters in the 34th Assembly District deserve to experience democracy and have their voices heard. I envision a New York where all people have the opportunity to thrive - to be able to live, learn, work and raise their families with dignity, safety and equity under healthy conditions. Please detail any specific policy proposals you may have that will affect the LGBT community. I see all issues through an intersectional lens, so nearly every issue disproportionately impacts the LGBTQIA+ community - particularly how it relates to discrimination and bias, including criminal justice, education, immigration, economic justice, healthcare, etc. Specifically, I strongly support repealing the Walking while Trans bill, which allows the NYPD to profile primarily black and Latinx trans women, who are often doing nothing more than walking down the street, as sex workers. I would go even further by supporting decriminalizing sex work. Sex work is work, and trans women of color in my community have been disproportionately targeted by the police, putting them in greater danger. In addition, I support ensuring that our healthcare system provides gender-affirming healthcare and that state-issued identification allows for individuals to self-identify a gender that may not be aligned with the gender assigned at birth. In addition, central to my education platform is mandating that all public schools offer comprehensive sex-ed, specifically ensuring that it is age-appropriate, medically accurate, culturally competent, and LGBTQ-affirming. I will utilize discretionary funds to support LGBTQIA+ organizations in the community and am committed to ensuring that my staff is diverse and that there is a strong advocate/liaison to the LGBTQIA+ community in my district office. Please explain any activities and/or experiences that demonstrate your commitment to the LGBT civil rights movement. Earlier this year, the Ali Forney Center was encountering some difficulties opening up a new supportive housing complex for homeless LGBT youth on 31st Avenue due to opposition from local homeowners. AFC has been operating out a church basement in the neighborhood for years, but was finally able to acquire a building from the church that would enable it provide real, long-term supportive housing services to the homeless LGBT youth population. Unfortunately, some Astoria residents objected to the project on the basis of typical anti-shelter hysteria. Our campaign organized a petition to collect signatures in support of the project from other locals and presented it at a public hearing of the Board of Standards and Appeals back in January in order to advocate for its approval. We collected nearly 200 signatures from, and brought about a dozen campaign supporters with us to the BSA to speak in favor of the project in person. I'm very pleased to report it was eventually approved, and construction has been cleared to begin (once the coronavirus outbreak permits, of course).

[PDF page 28] 2020 State Candidate Questionnaire Responses You can see footage of my remarks at the BSA hearing here: https://twitter.com/ZohranKMamdani/status/1226906815750905856 What experience do you have to demonstrate you are the best person to represent the office you seek? I was born and raised in Kampala, Uganda, and grew up in New York City after my family moved here when I was seven years old. I graduated from Bronx Science and now work as a foreclosure prevention housing counselor, helping immigrant families facing eviction stay in the homes they worked their whole lives to earn. Every day at work, I see the consequences of the pro-corporate and pro-landlord policies in Albany. They’ve turned family homes into investment properties while letting public housing fall into decay and disrepair. When people are drowning, the stopgap solutions that are available now, like small grants and low-interest loans, do nothing for the vast majority of New Yorkers struggling with housing insecurity. No matter how many families I’m able to help, there are always thousands more on the precipice of homelessness because of an unexpected illness, job loss, or emergency. The families I work with live mainly in Jackson Heights and Richmond Hill, but the same housing crisis is unfolding in Astoria. Since 2010, median rents in Astoria have increased by 30 percent to $2,200 per month - a startling figure totally beyond the reach of most New Yorkers. Just last year, there were 4,043 evictions in Queens, representing 20% of all evictions across the city. Astoria needs someone in Albany who not only knows first-hand the kind of pain and desperation that our families are experiencing, but knows what’s causing it as well. I do because I see it happening every day. That’s why I’m not accepting a penny from the corporations, real estate developers and special interest PACs that buy off politicians to support their bottom lines and insulate them from accountability. That’s why we’re building a truly grassroots campaign, supported by volunteers and funded by small-dollar donations. This is what’s going to allow us to speak the truth about what’s happening to our city and our state, and what has to be done to stop it. Please detail any specific policy proposals you may have that will affect the LGBT community. The foundational issues of our campaign are enacting a homes guarantee, establishing publicly owned utilities, and ending mass incarceration in New York - all of which bear directly upon the well-being of queer communities in our city and our state. Queer and trans people suffer disproportionately from housing

[PDF page 29] 2020 State Candidate Questionnaire Responses insecurity, financial precarity, and carceral violence at higher rates than their cis and straight peers. By guaranteeing robust public services, especially high-quality homes for all, we can remove the anxiety that so many queer people feel over whether or not they'll be able to live openly without endangering their access to employment, shelter, or financial security. By ending the specter of police and carceral violence, we can remove the anxiety that so many queer people feel over just walking down the street. This last point is especially pertinent in Queens County, which has seen more arrests for walking while trans than any other borough in recent years. We need to repeal the walking while trans ban and fully drecriminalize sex work, as trans women - especially migrant trans women of color - are some of those most impacted by criminalization. Yes Section 2: CANDIDATE EXPERIENCE (Short Answer) Please provide brief responses to each of the following questions - cite specific examples of your policy proposals and/or previous actions as applicable. Please explain any activities and/or experiences that demonstrate your commitment to the LGBT civil rights movement. As the only queer Asian-American woman and one of four Asian-Americans in the State legislature, I recognize how underrepresented women, LGBT and TGNC individuals, and people of color are. I have made it a priority to increase representation in politics and ensure that all voices can be included in policy-making through actively engaging marginalized communities and supporting pipelines to develop future leaders through mentorship and opportunities. Every year, I march at the NYC Pride Parade along with my staff and intern team, with many of us identifying ourselves as LGBT, queer, or non-gendering confirming. No New Yorker should be excluded from anything based on their sexual orientation or gender. This is why I am a proud sponsor of the Gender Expression Non-Discrimination Act (GENDA) which was signed into law last year. This law prohibits discrimination in employment, housing, public accomodations, and other areas. In these trying times, where our civil rights and protections are constantly

[PDF page 75] 2020 State Candidate Questionnaire Responses under attack, we will fight to protect and preserve the rights of our LGBTQIA community. Furthermore, I am one of the lead sponsors and helped introduce the Stop Violence in the Sex Trades Act (along with Sen. Salazar and Ramos and Assemblymember Gottfried) to decriminalize sex work in New York. I’ve worked with Decrim NY for two years to push that issue forward. This is an issue I deeply care about because it is LGBT and TGNC individuals, especially trans women of color, who are most criminalized and harmed by our current policies, and in my district, many Asian migrant women working in massage parlors are continuously harassed and assaulted by police officers for their work as well. I have also fought alongside Decrim NY to repeal what we call the Walking While Trans Ban. which unfairly targets people just for what they look like. As you might have seen, I have been an outspoken champion for the Child Victims Act which brings justice to survivors of childhood sexual abuse. This law amends our statutes adding five additional years for criminal charges to be brought and pushes the statute of limitations to permit civil actions to be brought up until the victim is 55. The law also includes a one year look-back window which began on August 14th for adult survivors, who under previous law, were unable to seek civil action. Many victims are still facing barriers to pursuing justice against their alleged abusers. In the upcoming session, we must fight to pass legislation to extend the look-back period for survivors and establish a child victims’ foundation fund which provides resources to help survivors throughout the legal process. Over the years, I have advocated for environmental changes and tenant’s rights. I have testified at City Council hearings for tenants right to counsel in housing court and have advocated for better air quality in the South Bronx. My understanding of the community and my experience has prepared me to represent the residents of Assembly District 79. Please detail any specific policy proposals you may have that will affect the LGBT community. One of my platforms is delivering equitable education to the residents of Assembly District 79 and around New York. In the South Bronx, students of color are disproportionately suspended at higher rates compared to their white counterparts. This includes LGBTQ+ students of color who are provoked because of bullying. If elected, I will push for more restorative justice alternatives to suspensions in schools and allocate funds for schools to create safe spaces for LGBTQ+ youth. Moreover, I want to push for the inclusion of more culturally responsive teaching, which includes teaching LGBTQ+ centered curriculum. Homelessness is a major issue facing residents of Assembly District 79 and this is because of the rising cost of rent and the lack of affordable housing in our district. Moreover, LGBTQ+ youth homelessness has skyrocketed and as a state we need to address these issues. In Albany, I will ensure enough funds are allocated to Transitional housing programs, to ensure Bronxites are able to break the cycle of homelessness. Recently, the Governor has proposed cuts to Medicaid, which residents of my district depend on for quality healthcare. If elected, I vow to not propose any cuts to medicaid because low income LGBTQ+ people depend on this resource to pay for much needed screenings and cover the cost of life saving prescription drugs. This pandemic has exposed the systemic failure of adequate and accessible healthcare to address longtime health comorbidities among black, brown, LGBTQ and other minority populations. This isn't a new trend, I've sounded the alarm about our medically underserved District for years. Now pressed by the media, some electeds say "the disparities are real and unfortunate" ... I say it's a national disgrace! Still, healthcare access has not improved, Staten Island still has no public hospital, and there are just two testing sites in the North Shore (one by appointment only). Coney Island Hospital, fortunately, continues to serve area residents. My parents taught me and my siblings, literally, to set a table for the poor and the castaway; so we would become "Champions" for the least of us. As such, I am a fierce advocate of worker's rights, economic security, and upholding Union guarantees. I am a TRUE Democrat and an unafraid "Voice for the Voiceless". I was born and raised in the West Brighton neighborhood of Staten Island. For several years, the Edwin Markham Gardens (NYCHA) was home. In so doing, I implemented mandated Worker protection programs, and trained Managers on best practices and supervision, worker education and protections. I am very proud of my reputation as an Intermediary and Problem Solver with Management, Unions and Employees. While a multi-purposed event, one takeaway of this expert panel of NINE Black Male Physicians, remains to excite and encourage young men of color to consider careers in medicine. During President Trump's 2019 budget shutdown - which caused millions of Federal employees to work without pay, including Coast Guard servicepersons - I was honored that my Dad, an 85 year old Coast Guard Veteran, joined me to deliver a truckload of groceries to Coast Guard families stationed at Fort Wadsworth, Staten Island. My ancestors, Black, White, Jewish, Christian, and Muslim, immigrated to the U.S., as have so many, in search of economic opportunities and for some to escape religious and political persecution. I am acutely aware of the sacrifices both my distant and near ancestors made to reach the United States and I am dedicated to ensuring this country remains a haven for those in need. From an early age I was inspired by music, I am a classically trained violinist and after graduating college I turned my love for music into a career becoming the owner of a recording studio. I worked with many talented, Brooklyn-based artists. However, in the summer of 2014, my life changed dramatically. While we all watched the death of Eric Garner with anger and frustration, one of my childhood friends was killed by the police. He was a gentle and kind human being who joined the Air Force after high school. He served for eight years, only to return home to lose his life at the hands of the police. These tragedies drove me to become a community organizer and activist. I volunteered for Jews for Racial and Economic Justice (JFREJ), serving as their liaison to Communities United for Police Reform. As an activist and community organizer I assisted to organize support for legislation that strengthened transparency and accountability for law enforcement including the Right to Know Act and the Police State Act. I am also a co-founder of JFREJ’s “Jews of Color” group. I went on to work for Senator Velmanette Montgomery (25thDistrict) as a Community Liaison where for nearly three years I was on the front lines serving the communities of the 25th District. From fighting for affordable housing to forming partnerships between city and state agencies and the community, to assisting NYCHA residents get needed repairs, I helped craft practical solutions to the district’s everyday problems. I have been on the front lines fighting for affordable housing and tenant rights as a vocal opponent of socially irresponsible developments that put profits over our community. I have helped tenants organize to demand repairs to their apartments and worked with local elected officials to draft legislation that promotes civics education in our schools.

[PDF page 124] 2020 State Candidate Questionnaire Responses Today, I am running on a platform centered around ending mass incarceration, addressing the affordable housing crisis, fighting for equity in our education system and ending the rampant social and economic chasm plaguing our society. My professional experience as both a community organizer and staffer for Senator Montgomer has provided me with a dual lens and experience- understanding the community I seek to represent along with the knowledge how bills get passed in Albany. Both provide me with the foundation to be an effective legislator and advocate for everyday New Yorkers in Albany. Please detail any specific policy proposals you may have that will affect the LGBT community. In the wake of the recent SCOTUS case addressing employment protections for LGBTQ+ communities we must redouble our efforts to continue the fight to protect and recognize the hard-won rights of the LGBTQ+ community. GENDA, a long fought-for law passed by the NYS Legislature in 2019, added gender identity and expression to the State’s human rights and hate laws and recognizes LGBTQ+ as a protected class. GENDA now prohibits discrimination in employment, housing, and public accommodations against the LGBTQ+ community. Now we must ensure that our government services and protections match these values and strengthen the law as we see weaknesses and loopholes in it that require closing. I will work closely with the LGBTQ+ community and advocacy organizations to craft regulations and legislation to make sure the promises of GENDA are kept. Since Trump took office there's been a significant uptick in violence against members of the transgender and gender non-conforming violence (TGNC) which disproportionately affects trans women of color. We need to ensure the State recognizes and validates these identities and provide a safer and braver space for New Yorkers to be themselves. If elected I will be a strong advocate for legislation that protects the LGBTQ+ community. State protections are increasingly important in the “Age of Trump'' where our federal courts are compromised by appointments of unqualified judges who are openly hostile to the LGBTQ+ community. The 77th precinct, which is in my district, has one of the highest rates of arrests for “Walking While Trans” in all of New York. I will not only prioritize passing legislation to repeal the “Walking While Trans” ban, but I will introduce legislation that enables those with prior

[PDF page 125] 2020 State Candidate Questionnaire Responses violations for Loitering for the Purpose of Prostitution violations and convictions to clear their records so that they can access employment. If elected, I will also work to decriminalize sex work. I recognize the disproportionate impact the criminal justice system can have on LGBTQ+ people, and I will push to restore recent bail reforms that were rolled back in the recent budget so that people like Layleen Polanco will not be unjustly incarcerated. Finally, I will vote in favor of legalizing surrogacy with protections for all participants. I am also concerned about LGBTQ+ youth who are disproportionately homeless or have to be removed from foster homes for abusive treatment. Despite the fact that New York has comprehensive legal protections (N.Y. Comp. Codes R. & Regs. tit. 14, § 527.8(d) and N.Y. Comp. Codes R. & Regs. tit. 11, § 52.16(2) in place to protect LGBTQI youth, 78% of homeless LBGTQ+ youth who have either run away or were removed from their homes report abuse and unacceptable treatment by the foster family. In the 2017 study, Safe Havens: Closing the Gap Between Recommended Practice and Reality for Transgender and Gender-Expansive Youth in Out-of-Home Care,” the Children’s Rights organization recommends that not only do we need legal and policy protections to encourage positive staff hiring, training and coaching practices, but we must also provide, “better support for families of origin and foster and adoptive parents; increased community collaboration; intentional engagement with LGBTQ+ young people to ensure that they are affirmed in care; and a commitment to agency-wide culture change” (Children’s Rights). The traditional model of gender separation does not work for a community of individuals who do not identify with a gender binary. LGBTQ+ youth need safe spaces that affirm their identity, with resource centers for runaway youth as well as for those struggling at home or in foster care. As a priority, these centers should support helping homeless youth get documentation so they can sign up for government services like Medicaid, provide public transportation access like metrocards, as well as appropriate physical and mental health services, crisis stabilization services, addiction treatment services or referrals (I support housing first), transitional housing, GED, Get College Ready, and skills/trade counselors and educators to help with educational and employment opportunities. These centers should re-create the type of supportive, home-like environment, like the model of the Ali Forney Center in NYC, to properly serve our youth. As a legislator I would want to work with advocacy groups and the experts in this field to devise new requirements such as foster family and supporting professionals

[PDF page 126] 2020 State Candidate Questionnaire Responses training along with other support systems that affirm this at-risk, vulnerable community. As a state legislator I would make it my mission to ensure that these youths are provided with the necessary resources and funding they need. Yes Section 2: CANDIDATE EXPERIENCE (Short Answer) Please provide brief responses to each of the following questions - cite specific examples of your policy proposals and/or previous actions as applicable. Please explain any activities and/or experiences that demonstrate your commitment to the LGBT civil rights movement. I am committed to fighting for equality and dignity for all New Yorkers. In New York State, when the Democrats took control of the New York State Senate for the first real time in almost 100 years, we made significant strides in establishing basic protections for the LGBT community. First and foremost, we passed GENDA to prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression and included gender identity and expression under hate crime law. GENDA was especially important because we added Transgender New Yorkers to those protected by the state’s Hate Crime Laws. In addition to passing GENDA, we passed a ban on conversion therapy,which was the morally and ethically next right thing to do, prohibiting mental health professionals from engaging in sexual orientation change efforts with a patient under the age of eighteen. These are basic protections, but they are a serious matter of acknowledging the humanity and dignity of all LGBT individuals. Moreover, we finally eliminated the “gay panic” defense, which which let murderers claim temporary insanity because they found out someone was gay or

[PDF page 151] 2020 State Candidate Questionnaire Responses transgender (S.6573 / Hoylman;) and made it possible for veterans who were discharged under Don’t Ask Don’t Tell to be eligible for veterans’ benefits (S.45B / Hoylman). I also am advocating for including a third gender option on state documents. What experience do you have to demonstrate you are the best person to represent the office you seek? As the democratic incumbent for the 34th state senate district, representing the Bronx & Westchester in Albany for the past 14 months, I realize that the most important core value that I carry with me into every meeting, event, and session on the floor is integrity and transparency. We have failed in almost every category when it comes to putting New Yorkers first. If we actually want to earn the title of public servants, we must start serving the public instead of the special interests who have been given the key to the castle for far too long. Yes, we’ve made progress on LGBT issues, housing issues, criminal justice reform, immigration issues, election reform, reproductive rights, sexual harassment, assault and rape laws, however, let us not be jaded or blinded by the progress we’ve made. Progress that was stalled for a decade, and progress that only brought us “current” so to speak. As we look towards the future, it is incumbent upon us to have a collective vision that brings New York forward, and let’s New York lead to its fullest potential. To do so requires embracing technology and the future of work, upending racism, sexism, and homophobia. Becoming a state where all zip codes are desirable to live in because the air is clean and the schools are good. Sure. We have made progress, but we have not taken the necessary step forward to lead. I am running for re-election to continue the work I have set out to accomplish in the New York State Senate, and to see the above mentioned vision to fruition. My desire to serve and my dedication to do what is right and just has only grown more deeply in my 14 months serving; and as Chairwoman of the Ethics Committee, my work is certainly far from done. I believe that our time as legislators is precious. We have an unknown amount of time serving, just like we have an unknown amount of time on this earth. That means that every issue I stand by, and every issue I fight for, is done with intense passion and urgency, because no one knows what tomorrow will bring. While serving, I have experienced some of the most disappointing days in my life -- but these days have often been followed by utter inspiration, motivation and a fervor to break down the walls erected to keep certain people, ideas, and laws alive. I believe these walls were made to be taken down by me, and my commitment to justice and a world that is equally accessible to everyone, has only grown stronger and louder during this time.

[PDF page 152] 2020 State Candidate Questionnaire Responses As a representative of the Bronx, I have witnessed devastating poverty, homelessness, overdose rates, and an underinvestment in its neighborhoods and its future, across almost every single categorical vertical that exists (education, job growth, health care, housing). I have seen people of color arrested on offenses that in other communities would be written off as a warning. I have witnessed survivors of human trafficking, transforming their pain to fight to save the young women being trafficked in the Bronx. I have watched as corporations set up shop in the posh streets of “SoBro”, or the South Bronx, only to take more from the people who have been given the least -- only to drive a thousand more trucks on their streets and make their air more likely to cause them asthma and in some cases, death. I have experienced our healthcare system being torn down during a pandemic, not because we were not prepared as a city or a state, but because cuts were made to “save money” in the areas that had the most need. This behavior and so much more, keeps me fighting for every single resident of District 34, and keeps me focused on the progress that we must make. I still also believe in FDR’s Four Freedoms -- freedom of speech and expression, freedom of religion, freedom from want, and freedom from fear -- and that these freedoms clearly define the bedrock principles of progressivism. These principles call us to ensure access to housing, healthcare, education, safety in our communities, self-determination, and more for every single human being. Applied today, I would include ending the politics of exclusion; harnessing the potential power of government for the good of all; and eliminating the outsized influence of money and corporate interests in campaigning and in the creation and passage of public policies. As COVID- 19 mercilessly sweeps through our City and through the District, our communities of color are disproportionately affected with tragic outcomes that far outnumber non-minority neighborhoods. This pandemic has exposed the systemic failure of adequate and accessible healthcare to address longtime health comorbidities among black, brown, LGBTQ and other minority populations. Tragically the death toll in New York City increases daily by the hundreds, and yet, in our densely populated neighborhoods, untold individuals succumb unreported and unknown. This isn't a new trend, I've sounded the alarm about our medically underserved District for years. Now pressed by the media, some electeds say "the disparities are real and unfortunate" ... I say it's a national disgrace! Still, healthcare access has not improved, Staten Island still has no public hospital, and there are just two testing sites in the North Shore (one by appointment only). Coney Island Hospital, fortunately, continues to serve area residents. My parents taught me and my siblings, literally, to set a table for the poor and the castaway; so we would become "Champions" for the least of us. As such, I am a fierce advocate of worker's rights, economic security, and upholding Union guarantees. I am a TRUE Democrat and an unafraid "Voice for the Voiceless". I was born and raised in the West Brighton neighborhood of Staten Island. For several years, the Edwin Markham Gardens (NYCHA) was home. "The Markham Homes" was a multicultural community of 360 working class families with dreams to thrive, and not to simply exist. For over 30 years as a Human Resources Professional, I have battled Economic Injustice, by connecting the unemployed and underemployed, Veterans, LGBTQ individuals, and Homeless or Sheltered persons, to hundreds of full time jobs. I exposed oppressive policies aimed to diminish Worker Protections and Labor Unions. In so doing, I implemented mandated Worker protection programs, and trained Managers on best practices and supervision, worker education and protections. I am very proud of my reputation as an Intermediary and Problem Solver with Management, Unions and Employees. Community Health Education: To address the disparities in both health outcomes and healthcare access across the 23rd District, I hosted, "Ask The Doctors", a community wellness forum. While a multi-purposed event, one takeaway of this expert panel of NINE Black Male Physicians, remains to excite and encourage young men of color to consider careers in medicine. The Physicians of "Ask The Doctors" are fully cognizant of the detriment caused by the barriers to access and

[PDF page 7] 2020 State Candidate Questionnaire Responses ability to pay for health care, oft-times, life saving medical care. The forums only convene in communities of color and attempt to break through the biases and microaggressions so often exhibited in many Patient/Doctor experiences. Attendees were encouraged to ask the questions that they don't or wouldn't ask, or questions that providers ignore. Tenant Association Presidents in Coney Island called ME when their community food pantries were bare, and I delivered! During President Trump's 2019 budget shutdown - which caused millions of Federal employees to work without pay, including Coast Guard servicepersons - I was honored that my Dad, an 85 year old Coast Guard Veteran, joined me to deliver a truckload of groceries to Coast Guard families stationed at Fort Wadsworth, Staten Island. As a true Leader, I know how and when to lead from within. Let me assure everyone, it's ok to serve humanity, especially the least of us. It's ok to show compassion and to show that that you really care. Please detail any specific policy proposals you may have that will affect the LGBT community. Seamless and Fearless Health and Mental Health Access! The 23rd District is Federally designated as Medically Underserved. The lack of medical access has lead to poorer health outcomes, patient fear and guilt, and even refusal by providers - especially regarding our LGBTQ neighbors. I support the New York Health program, a comprehensive and universal single-payer system of access to health insurance for ALL New York State residents. Staten Island is the only borough without a public hospital. I would legislate permanent changes to the Indigent Care Pool to insure that our safety-net hospitals remain in operation, like Richmond University Medical Center. I will fight against 2020 cuts to funding of healthcare delivery, specifically of Medicaid, which is critically vital to the health and welfare of 'the least of us', yes the marginalized Black and Brown folks, LGBTQ folks, and Seniors. I am a member of Lambda Independent Democrats and Stonewall Democrats and attend many of their meetings and events as well as the Jim Owles club. I support LGBTQ+ civil and social rights and see the LGBTQ+ community as being an integral part of the American fabric and Senate District 25. Regarding issues that face the LGBTQ+ community that I now support and will actively advocate for as a legislator is, the decriminalization of sex work, repealing the “Walking While Trans Statute, passing the gender recognition act, and focusing on providing safe spaces for LGBTQ+ youth, which includes housing, mental health services and educational opportunities. Importantly, LGBTQ+ elders will always be included in my advocacy. What experience do you have to demonstrate you are the best person to represent the office you seek? I am a life-long resident of the 25th District 25 which I seek to represent in the NYS Senate.I was born and raised in the district. I have a demonstrated commitment to the district and to everyday New Yorkers. I am in the unique position to bring

[PDF page 12] 2020 State Candidate Questionnaire Responses diverse populations to the table to create an inclusive campaign, centered around racial and economic justice. I am a progressive Democrat whose family history in the district dates back 70 years. My ancestors, Black, White, Jewish, Christian, and Muslim, immigrated to the U.S., as have so many, in search of economic opportunities and for some to escape religious and political persecution. I am acutely aware of the sacrifices both my distant and near ancestors made to reach the United States and I am dedicated to ensuring this country remains a haven for those in need. From an early age I was inspired by music, I am a classically trained violinist and after graduating college I turned my love for music into a career becoming the owner of a recording studio. I worked with many talented, Brooklyn-based artists. However, in the summer of 2014, my life changed dramatically. While we all watched the death of Eric Garner with anger and frustration, one of my childhood friends was killed by the police. He was a gentle and kind human being who joined the Air Force after high school. He served for eight years, only to return home to lose his life at the hands of the police. These tragedies drove me to become a community organizer and activist. I volunteered for Jews for Racial and Economic Justice (JFREJ), serving as their liaison to Communities United for Police Reform. As an activist and community organizer I assisted to organize support for legislation that strengthened transparency and accountability for law enforcement including the Right to Know Act and the Police State Act. I am also a co-founder of JFREJ’s “Jews of Color” group. I went on to work for Senator Velmanette Montgomery (25thDistrict) as a Community Liaison where for nearly three years I was on the front lines serving the communities of the 25th District. From fighting for affordable housing to forming partnerships between city and state agencies and the community, to assisting NYCHA residents get needed repairs, I helped craft practical solutions to the district’s everyday problems. I have been on the front lines fighting for affordable housing and tenant rights as a vocal opponent of socially irresponsible developments that put profits over our community. I have helped tenants organize to demand repairs to their apartments and worked with local elected officials to draft legislation that promotes civics education in our schools.

[PDF page 13] 2020 State Candidate Questionnaire Responses Today, I am running on a platform centered around ending mass incarceration, addressing the affordable housing crisis, fighting for equity in our education system and ending the rampant social and economic chasm plaguing our society. My professional experience as both a community organizer and staffer for Senator Montgomer has provided me with a dual lens and experience- understanding the community I seek to represent along with the knowledge how bills get passed in Albany. Both provide me with the foundation to be an effective legislator and advocate for everyday New Yorkers in Albany. Please detail any specific policy proposals you may have that will affect the LGBT community. In the wake of the recent SCOTUS case addressing employment protections for LGBTQ+ communities we must redouble our efforts to continue the fight to protect and recognize the hard-won rights of the LGBTQ+ community. GENDA, a long fought-for law passed by the NYS Legislature in 2019, added gender identity and expression to the State’s human rights and hate laws and recognizes LGBTQ+ as a protected class. GENDA now prohibits discrimination in employment, housing, and public accommodations against the LGBTQ+ community. Now we must ensure that our government services and protections match these values and strengthen the law as we see weaknesses and loopholes in it that require closing. I will work closely with the LGBTQ+ community and advocacy organizations to craft regulations and legislation to make sure the promises of GENDA are kept. Since Trump took office there's been a significant uptick in violence against members of the transgender and gender non-conforming violence (TGNC) which disproportionately affects trans women of color. We need to ensure the State recognizes and validates these identities and provide a safer and braver space for New Yorkers to be themselves. If elected I will be a strong advocate for legislation that protects the LGBTQ+ community. State protections are increasingly important in the “Age of Trump'' where our federal courts are compromised by appointments of unqualified judges who are openly hostile to the LGBTQ+ community. The 77th precinct, which is in my district, has one of the highest rates of arrests for “Walking While Trans” in all of New York. I will not only prioritize passing legislation to repeal the “Walking While Trans” ban, but I will introduce legislation that enables those with prior

[PDF page 14] 2020 State Candidate Questionnaire Responses violations for Loitering for the Purpose of Prostitution violations and convictions to clear their records so that they can access employment. If elected, I will also work to decriminalize sex work. I recognize the disproportionate impact the criminal justice system can have on LGBTQ+ people, and I will push to restore recent bail reforms that were rolled back in the recent budget so that people like Layleen Polanco will not be unjustly incarcerated. Finally, I will vote in favor of legalizing surrogacy with protections for all participants. I am also concerned about LGBTQ+ youth who are disproportionately homeless or have to be removed from foster homes for abusive treatment. Codes R. & Regs. tit. 11, § 52.16(2) in place to protect LGBTQI youth, 78% of homeless LBGTQ+ youth who have either run away or were removed from their homes report abuse and unacceptable treatment by the foster family. What experience do you have to demonstrate you are the best person to represent the office you seek? My family’s lived in Prospect Heights (the center of the district) for three generations - this is my community and I know its struggles. In 2017, when I ran for City Council in the overlapping neighborhoods, I earned the votes of over 9,000 people in these neighborhoods, despite running on an independent line. The issues that most seriously affect the LGBTQ community are homelessness, job discrimination, and access to competent healthcare including competent healthcare. In addition, the most vulnerable members of our community are subject to violence by police and others, while their basic means of maintaining a living are criminalized. These major structural programs have to be addressed by aggressive reform. I believe that queer legislators have a responsibility to talk about solutions to the problems facing our community, for example talking about how expanding healthcare access expands access to PReP and other HIV treatment, or talking about access to hormones for transgender people could be significantly expanded unders such a system. No one should have to go to Callen-Lorde or APICHA and find themselves turned away due to capacity and drug shortages. We need to expand mental health access, offer more affordable housing to keep our youth out of shelters and off the streets when they are kicked out of their homes, and expand access to good jobs. I will also support Senate Bill S56B, which ensures that all New Yorkers, including transgender and non-binary New Yorkers, can get identity documents, like passports and birth certificates, that align with their gender identity. As Chair of the Senate Corrections Committee, I have been leading the charge for extensive prison reform that would make our prison system more humane and genuinely rehabilitative. This year I am fighting for parole reform, expanding prison education programs, and ending solitary confinement with my bill, the HALT Solitary Confinement Act, which would restrict solitary confinement in NYS prisons and require alternative, more humane rehabilitation methods that don’t constitute as torture by UN standards. I have dedicated myself to advocating for progressive policies and I believe that the record that I have established underscores this dedication. My office has also established a well-known reputation in the district for providing wide-ranging, top- notch constituent services to our constituents most in need -- a crucial aspect of our role as public servants. I am proud to represent my Bronx community in the legislature, and I would be honored to continue doing so for another term.
